h1: The 6 Best Bluetooth Trackers for Android of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Android Bluetooth Trackers: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 Bluetooth trackers for Android phones scored on Google Find Hub support, ring volume and battery, from tags to wallet cards.
summary: The Lifemate Air Tracker is the best Android tag overall, combining Google Find Hub, up to 120 dB of sound and a 150 m range with no subscription. MiLi's single tag adds voice-command ringing and a year of CR2032 battery life. For value, XJQX's two-pack ships with spare cells, and UGREEN's rechargeable four-pack covers the whole family. Choose the Ajblg card for a wallet, or Life360 Tile if your household includes iPhones.
intro: Android owners have a quiet advantage in the tracker market that few buyers use: Google Find Hub turns the world's Android phones into a relay network, and it works with tags that cost a fraction of an Apple accessory. The catch is that the listing has to say Find Hub, not just Bluetooth, or the tag will sit in your drawer as an expensive beeper.

We reviewed six Android-ready trackers from their listings and scored them on the Primea framework. Network compatibility came first, followed by how loud each one rings, how its battery behaves and whether its shape suits keys, bags or a wallet. Phone requirements matter too, because several of these need Android 9 or later.

products.name: Lifemate Air Tracker Tags for Android
products.verdict: Find Hub support, a loud 120 dB ring and a long 150 m range, with no subscription.
products.description:
Lifemate builds directly around Google Find Hub on Android 9 or later, which is the right foundation for an Android tag. Its sound reaches up to 120 dB, the loudest figure in this ranking, and the quoted Bluetooth range is 150 m (500 ft) in open air. It is dust and water resistant, with a water test of 30 minutes at 3 feet, and has no subscription fee.

It beats the MiLi on loudness and the listed water testing, though the MiLi counters with voice-command ringing. Against the XJQX, you trade the included spare batteries for stronger documented durability.

A strong everyday pick for keys, backpacks and bikes. The caveat is that an open-air range figure shrinks fast through walls, so treat 150 m as a ceiling, not a promise, indoors.
products.idealFor: Android users wanting a loud, durable all-purpose tag.
products.skipIf: Anyone in your household uses an iPhone.

products.name: MiLi Air Tracker Tags for Android, 1 Pack
products.verdict: Rings on a voice command and carries IP67 protection, with a CR2032 good for about a year.
products.description:
MiLi's tag works through Google Find Hub on Android 9 or later and shares the same 150 m (500 ft) Bluetooth range as the Lifemate. What sets it apart is voice-command ringing, so you can ask your phone assistant to sound the tag without opening an app. It carries an IP67 rating and runs on a replaceable CR2032 for up to 1 year.

It ranks second because the listing gives no decibel figure, so you cannot compare loudness with the Lifemate. Compared with the XJQX, it offers sturdier rated protection but only a single tag in the box.

A good match for people who like hands-free finding. The caveat is that a single-tag pack leaves you buying more if you want to cover keys, a bag and a bike.
products.idealFor: Android owners who like asking an assistant to ring their keys.
products.skipIf: You want several tags in one order.

products.name: XJQX 2-Pack Bluetooth Tracker Tags for Android
products.verdict: Two tags, four batteries and two silicone cases, so the box is ready to use on day one.
products.description:
XJQX packs two tags, black and white, with four CR2032 cells in the box: two installed and two spare. It runs on Google Find Hub, with a 105 dB alarm and a quoted Bluetooth range of 350 ft. Two silicone key cases come included, which solves the question of how to attach a flat tag to a ring.

It sits third because the alarm is quieter than the Lifemate's 120 dB and the range is shorter than 150 m. On the other hand, nothing else in the roundup includes spare cells and cases, which makes the first year cheaper to run.

The pick for two items on a modest budget. Caveat: the spec sheet does not give a water rating, so keep it away from rain-soaked pockets.
products.idealFor: Android owners tagging keys plus one more item.
products.skipIf: You need a stated waterproof rating.

products.name: UGREEN Finder Duo Air Tracker Tags 4 Pack
products.verdict: Four USB-C rechargeable tags that also support Apple, handy for a split household.
products.description:
UGREEN's pack offers four rechargeable tags, each claimed to last 365 days per charge and charged over USB-C. Unusually, the listing says the tags work with either Apple Find My or Google Find Hub, so a household with one iPhone and one Android phone can share a set. Lost Mode and alerts are included, and communication is end-to-end encrypted.

It ranks fourth because the listing does not quote a ring volume or water rating, and a rechargeable cell means a yearly plug-in. Against the XJQX, you lose spare coin cells but gain two more tags and the Apple option.

Good for families who track bags, bikes and keys. Caveat: each tag is set up for one network, so decide which phone it belongs to before pairing.

products.name: Ajblg Wallet Tracker Card 2 Pack for Android
products.verdict: Two ultra-thin cards with an IP68 rating, made specifically for Android wallets.
products.description:
Ajblg ships two ultra-thin tracker cards that slide into a wallet slot, each rated IP68 and sounding an 80 to 100 dB buzzer. They report through Google Find Hub on Android 9 or later and, importantly, the listing says they do not support iOS. That clarity prevents the classic mistake of buying an Android card for an iPhone.

It ranks fifth since a card is only good for wallets, passports or luggage tags, and a buzzer of 80 to 100 dB is quieter than the round tags above. Compared with the Lifemate, you give up volume for a slim form.

A smart buy if your wallet is the item you lose. Caveat: the quiet buzzer is easily muffled inside a bag or pocket, so it is best used for fast checks in a room.
products.idealFor: Android users who keep losing their wallet or a passport pouch.
products.skipIf: You want to attach a tracker to keys or a backpack.

products.name: Life360 Tile Bluetooth Tracker, iOS and Android
products.verdict: Works on both phone platforms and rings your phone, but uses Tile's own network.
products.description:
Tile is the only tag in this list that runs on its own app and network instead of Google Find Hub, and it works on both iOS and Android. It can ring your phone even when the handset is silenced, and adds a discreet SOS alert and a Life360 family map. A 1-pack in black is the version listed.

It finishes last for an Android-specific ranking because the Find Hub tags tap Google's relay network, which is larger for Android users than Tile's crowd. What it offers in return is cross-platform flexibility and extra safety features.

Pick it when your partner or child carries an iPhone. Caveat: you will install the Tile app, and the richest features depend on Life360 membership options.
products.idealFor: Families split between iPhone and Android.
products.skipIf: You want the biggest Android relay network.

methodology.description: Tags that report through Google Find Hub on Android 9 or later scored highest, since that network is where most Android phones can help locate a lost tag.

whatMatters.detail: Find Hub lets nearby Android phones anonymously relay a tag's location to you, so the tag works far beyond Bluetooth range. Confirm that the listing names Google Find Hub and gives a minimum Android version, such as Android 9 or later, before you buy.

Louder alarms are easier to hear through cushions and bags. A 120 dB tag like the Lifemate cuts through noise better than an 80 to 100 dB buzzer. Look for an actual decibel number in the listing, not just a claim of a loud alarm.

Range is how far your phone can talk to the tag directly, measured in open air. Walls and bodies cut it sharply. Treat 150 m or 350 ft as a best case, and rely on Find Hub's relay network for anything beyond your own home.

A replaceable CR2032 lasts around a year and is easy to swap, while a rechargeable tag like the UGREEN needs a USB-C top-up. Spare cells in the box, as on the XJQX, avoid the first-year scramble. Check whether the battery is replaceable.

Keys, bikes and bags get wet. An IP67 or IP68 rating tells you how the tag was sealed, while a vague water-resistant label tells you little. Look for the IP number or a stated test, like Lifemate's 30 minutes at 3 feet.

faq.q: Do these trackers work on any Android phone?
faq.a: Most listings require Android 9 or later for Google Find Hub, including the Lifemate, MiLi and Ajblg. The Life360 Tile uses its own app, so it has different requirements. Check your phone's Android version in Settings before buying.

faq.q: What is the common mistake with Android trackers?
faq.a: Buying an Apple-only tag, or an Android-only card for an iPhone. The Ajblg card explicitly says it does not support iOS, and the Lifemate is built for Android, so read the supported platform first.

faq.q: Is the Lifemate worth it over cheaper packs?
faq.a: Yes if you want loudness and documented durability. It reaches 120 dB and lists a 30 minute, 3 foot water test, while the XJQX two-pack tops out at 105 dB with no water rating given.

faq.q: How do I set up a Find Hub tracker?
faq.a: Insert the battery or power the tag, open Google Find Hub on your phone and follow the pairing prompt. The MiLi and Lifemate use this flow, and you can then ring the tag or see its last known location.

faq.q: How often should I replace the battery?
faq.a: The MiLi's CR2032 is rated up to a year, and the XJQX ships with spare cells. For the UGREEN rechargeables, plug into USB-C about once a year. Check battery status in the app before long trips.

faq.q: Can I track a tag far from home?
faq.a: Yes, through Find Hub's relay network, as long as other Android phones pass near the tag. The 150 m Lifemate range only applies to direct Bluetooth, so beyond your home it relies on crowd coverage.

finalTake: The Lifemate Air Tracker is the strongest all-round Android tag in this ranking because it pairs a very loud alarm with documented water testing and Google Find Hub support. The MiLi is the better fit for voice-command users, and the XJQX is the cheapest way to start with two tags. Confirm Find Hub support first, then choose the shape and battery that suit your things.
